# 11 U.S.C. §362(a), (k) — automatic stay

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §362(a)(1), (a)(6), (k)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) A petition operates as a stay, applicable to all entities, of— (1) the commencement or continuation of an action or proceeding against the debtor to recover a claim that arose before the commencement of the case; … **(6) any act to collect, assess, or recover a claim against the debtor that arose before the commencement of the case**. **(k)** An individual injured by any willful violation of a stay shall recover actual damages, including costs and attorneys' fees, and, in appropriate circumstances, punitive damages. Courts also sanction corporate debtors' creditors for willful violations under §105. Dunning letters, collection calls and threats to report to credit bureaus after the petition are acts to collect.
===== bc_502d_setoff.md =====
# 11 U.S.C. §502(d); setoff and recoupment

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §502(d); §553  
*Status in this library:* in force

§502(d): the court shall disallow any claim of an entity from which property is recoverable under §547 (preference) unless the entity has paid the amount for which it is liable. A creditor with preference exposure may find its claim disallowed until it returns the preference. Setoff of pre-petition mutual debts requires relief from stay.

# 11 U.S.C. §503(b)(9) and §546(c) — 20-day goods; reclamation

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §503(b)(9); §546(c)(1)  
*Status in this library:* in force

§503(b)(9): administrative expense for **the value of any goods received by the debtor within 20 days before the date of commencement** of a case in which the goods have been sold to the debtor in the ordinary course of the debtor's business. **Services, freight and handling are not 'goods'.** §546(c): a seller of goods may reclaim goods received by the debtor while insolvent within 45 days before the petition, by written demand not later than 45 days after receipt (or 20 days after the petition if the 45 days expire after commencement); reclamation is subject to prior liens (here the DIP lender's blanket lien).

# 11 U.S.C. §547(b), (c)(2), (c)(4), (g) — preferences

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §547  
*Status in this library:* in force

(b) The trustee may avoid any transfer of an interest of the debtor in property— (1) to or for the benefit of a creditor; (2) for or on account of an antecedent debt; (3) made while the debtor was insolvent (presumed during the 90 days, §547(f)); (4) made **on or within 90 days before the date of the filing**; (5) that enables the creditor to receive more than in a chapter 7 liquidation. **(c)(2) Ordinary course:** the trustee may not avoid a transfer to the extent it was in payment of a debt incurred in the ordinary course and the transfer was made **(A) in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of the debtor and the transferee, or (B) according to ordinary business terms**. Payments made under **shortened terms, pressure, or unusual methods (wire on demand) compared with the parties' history** generally fall outside (c)(2)(A). **(c)(4) New value:** to the extent that, after such transfer, the creditor gave new value to or for the benefit of the debtor not secured and on account of which the debtor did not make an otherwise unavoidable transfer. (g) The creditor bears the burden on (c) defenses.

# Critical vendor orders — practice note

*Citation:* *In re Kmart Corp.*, 359 F.3d 866 (7th Cir. 2004); Dkt. 44 in this case  
*Status in this library:* in force

A debtor may seek authority to pay certain pre-petition claims of vendors whose continued supply is essential and who cannot be replaced; the vendor must typically agree to customary trade terms for the case. Being designated a critical vendor is the legitimate route to early payment of pre-petition claims; it is at the debtor's discretion and the court's approval.

# Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002, 3003 — proofs of claim; bar date

*Citation:* Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3003(c)(2)-(3); 3002(c)  
*Status in this library:* in force

In a chapter 11 case, a creditor whose claim is not scheduled or is scheduled as disputed, contingent or unliquidated **must file a proof of claim** by the bar date fixed by the court; a creditor who fails to do so shall not be treated as a creditor for purposes of voting and distribution. Late claims are allowed only on a showing of excusable neglect (*Pioneer*). A §503(b)(9) request is typically made by motion or by the procedure the bar-date order specifies, and should be asserted separately from the general unsecured claim.

| 2025-05-29 | 42,500 | MS-7355 | 46 | 285 | ACH | no |

| 2025-08-14 | 38,700 | MS-7451 | 43 | 208 | ACH | no |
| 2025-09-25 | 45,200 | MS-7498 | 47 | 166 | ACH | no |

| 2026-02-26 | MS-7802 | 6,900 | after Feb 10 |

| 2026-03-09 | MS-7819 | 14,400 | after Feb 10 and Feb 27 |

| Scenario | Arithmetic | Exposure |
|---|---|---:|
| A — ordinary-course fails on Feb 10 + Feb 27; new value credit includes the 20-day goods | 85,000 − 99,400 → 0 | **$0** |
| B — as A, but 20-day goods that carry §503(b)(9) status cannot also count as new value (a real split in the case law, **not covered by the library → [unverified]**) | 85,000 − (99,400 − 78,100) = 85,000 − 21,300 | **$63,700** |

## 5. Open / unreconciled items (deliberately left open)

1. The bar-date notice is internally inconsistent: it is **dated 2026-04-02**, i.e. 14 days in the future as of today, and it recites a critical-vendor hearing on the same date (2026-04-02). The bar date of 2026-06-11 is used as stated, but the operative order must be confirmed.
2. No separate §503(b)(9) deadline appears in the notice; the library says the request is made "by motion or by the procedure the bar-date order specifies" — that order is not in the file.
3. Whether Redwood asserts a claim against Mesa (the "you owe us" remark in the collection log) is unresolved; it would affect setoff under §553 (which needs stay relief) and the net claim amount.
4. No post-petition deliveries appear in the file (last delivery 2026-03-09). If Mesa has shipped since 2026-03-10, those amounts are outside §503(b)(9) and the library has no authority covering payment for post-petition goods **[unverified]**.
5. No returns, credits, disputes or warranty claims are recorded; if any exist, the 125,000 must be reduced.

# Advice to the CEO — Mesa Steel Supply / Redwood Fabrication (Chapter 11, filed 2026-03-10)

Plain English. Prepared 2026-03-19, nine days after the filing. Every legal point is backed by a file in
`library/INDEX.md`; anything the library does not cover is flagged **[unverified]**.

Bottom line: **you will not get paid first by filing papers. You get paid by (a) qualifying $78,100 as a
post-petition-priority "20-day goods" administrative claim, and (b) being named a critical vendor by Redwood and
the court.** Right now the biggest risk to that outcome is our own collection department, and the second biggest is
that Redwood's estate may come at us for **up to $85,000** of the money we received in February.

---

## 1. What Mesa must stop doing today, and why

**Stop, effective immediately and in writing to every person in AR and credit:**

1. **No more dunning letters, emails or calls** to Redwood asking for money.
2. **No credit-bureau reporting** and no threats to report.
3. **No threats to hold shipments as leverage** for the old balance. (Deciding prospectively not to sell without
   current terms is a commercial decision; demanding payment of the pre-filing balance in exchange for shipping is
   collection activity.)
4. **No liens, no lawsuits, no garnishment, no offsetting** of deposits or credit balances against the old balance.
   Setting off pre-bankruptcy mutual debts requires the court's permission (library/bc_502d_setoff.md).
5. **Do not accept any money from Redwood** on the old invoices. A payment of a pre-filing debt without court
   authority can be undone, and it would put us back in the preference line of fire.
6. **All contact goes through counsel** to Redwood's counsel. Nobody from AR talks to Redwood AP again.
7. **Preserve everything** — the collection log, the terms email, wire records. Litigation hold today. Do not
   "tidy up" the log.

**Why.** When Redwood filed, an automatic stay went into effect against everyone. It stops "any act to collect,
assess, or recover a claim against the debtor that arose before" the filing, and the library says flatly that
"dunning letters, collection calls and threats to report to credit bureaus after the petition are acts to collect"
(library/bc_362.md). A creditor who **willfully** violates the stay pays actual damages, costs and attorneys' fees,
and punitive damages in appropriate circumstances; the library also notes courts **sanction corporate creditors**
under §105 (the §362(k) damages text refers to an "individual" — Redwood is a company, so the §105 route is the one
that bites here).

We have already done three of these things, and they are documented in our own collection log:

| Date | Act | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-03-12 | "FINAL NOTICE — pay **$210,000** within 5 days or we refer to collections" (mailed + emailed), two days after the filing | Stay violation. Worse, the number was wrong: we invoiced $210,000 since 2026-01-12 but **$85,000 was already paid**, so the true open balance was $125,000. We demanded money twice over. |
| 2026-03-15 | Collection call to Redwood AP; we were told on the call "we filed Chapter 11, talk to counsel"; the reply recorded in our log was "that's not our problem, you owe us" | High risk: this is knowledge of the case plus a continued demand. |
| 2026-03-18 | Email to Redwood's CFO threatening to "hold all future shipments and report to credit bureaus" | Highest risk: credit-bureau threats are named in the library as acts to collect, and it was sent after we knew about the case. |

Whether the March 12 letter was "willful" is arguable — it is not established in the file that anyone knew about the
filing on that date, and the library does not define "willful" **[unverified]**. The March 15 and March 18 acts were
after Redwood told us. Damages here are usually attorneys' fees and a sanction, not $125,000 — but it is a real,
self-inflicted cost, it is exactly the kind of thing that makes a debtor refuse to make us a critical vendor, and it
gives the estate leverage in the preference negotiation discussed next.

The single most valuable thing we can do today is send a written stand-down instruction and keep it. That is the
difference between "our AR clerk lost control of one account" and "Mesa's management condoned collection after
notice."

## 2. The money, correctly

| Bucket | Amount | What it means |
|---|---:|---|
| Total pre-filing claim | **$125,000** | Goods and services delivered 2026-02-04 → 2026-03-09, net of payments |
| "20-day goods" administrative claim, §503(b)(9) | **$78,100** | Steel received in the 20 days before filing (MS-7788 $41,300 on 2026-02-20; MS-7815 $36,800 on 2026-03-04). This is the strongest claim we have — an administrative expense, not a general unsecured claim (library/bc_503b9_546c.md) |
| General unsecured | **$46,900** | MS-7740 balance $25,600 (goods received 34 days before filing — outside the 20-day window) + freight $6,900 + on-site cutting services $14,400. Freight and services are **not** "goods" and cannot be dressed up as administrative (library/bc_503b9_546c.md) |

Reclamation (demanding the steel back under §546(c)): **available but nearly worthless.** We could demand return of
$103,700 of goods received in the 45 days before filing, but the written demand must be served by **2026-03-30** and
the right is subject to prior liens — the DIP lender has a blanket lien in this case (library/bc_503b9_546c.md).
Serve the demand because it is cheap and it is leverage in the critical-vendor conversation; do not count on the steel.

## 3. What Mesa may owe Redwood (yes, owe)

In a bankruptcy the estate can claw back payments a supplier received in the **90 days before filing** as
"preferences" — 2025-12-10 through 2026-03-10 in our case. Insolvency in that window is presumed against Redwood, so
we assume that element goes against us (library/bc_547.md).

We received **$180,000** in that window:

| Payment | Amount | Days after invoice | Method | Our read |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 2025-12-18 | $51,000 | 45 | ACH | **Protected** — normal for us |
| 2026-01-22 | $44,000 | 43 | ACH | **Protected** — normal for us |
| 2026-02-10 | $48,200 | 29 | ACH | **Exposed** — after we cut terms to NET 15 |
| 2026-02-27 | $36,800 | 25 | **WIRE we demanded** | **Exposed** — pressure + unusual method |

Our whole prior year was 43–47 days after invoice, always ACH, on net-45 terms. Then our credit department sent the
2026-01-20 email moving Redwood to **NET 15** and demanding "oldest open invoice first". The library is direct:
payments made under shortened terms, pressure, or unusual methods (wire on demand) compared with the parties' history
generally fall outside the ordinary-course defence (library/bc_547.md). So roughly **$95,000 protected / $85,000
exposed**. And we carry the burden of proving those defences, not Redwood (library/bc_547.md §547(g)).

The good news is the **new value** defence: after those two dangerous payments we kept shipping on credit —
$99,400 of goods and services (2026-02-20 onward) that Redwood never paid for. New value given after a payment and
not paid for reduces preference exposure dollar for dollar (library/bc_547.md §547(c)(4)). $99,400 against $85,000 of
exposure means the honest estimate of what we owe is **about zero**.

Two caveats, stated as they are:

  exposure rises to about **$63,700**. The library does not address that question **[unverified]**.

# 11 U.S.C. §362(a), (k) — automatic stay

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §362(a)(1), (a)(6), (k)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) A petition operates as a stay, applicable to all entities, of— (1) the commencement or continuation of an action or proceeding against the debtor to recover a claim that arose before the commencement of the case; … **(6) any act to collect, assess, or recover a claim against the debtor that arose before the commencement of the case**. **(k)** An individual injured by any willful violation of a stay shall recover actual damages, including costs and attorneys' fees, and, in appropriate circumstances, punitive damages. Courts also sanction corporate debtors' creditors for willful violations under §105. Dunning letters, collection calls and threats to report to credit bureaus after the petition are acts to collect.

=== bc_503b9_546c.md ===
# 11 U.S.C. §503(b)(9) and §546(c) — 20-day goods; reclamation

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §503(b)(9); §546(c)(1)  
*Status in this library:* in force

§503(b)(9): administrative expense for **the value of any goods received by the debtor within 20 days before the date of commencement** of a case in which the goods have been sold to the debtor in the ordinary course of the debtor's business. **Services, freight and handling are not 'goods'.** §546(c): a seller of goods may reclaim goods received by the debtor while insolvent within 45 days before the petition, by written demand not later than 45 days after receipt (or 20 days after the petition if the 45 days expire after commencement); reclamation is subject to prior liens (here the DIP lender's blanket lien).

=== bc_547.md ===
# 11 U.S.C. §547(b), (c)(2), (c)(4), (g) — preferences

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §547  
*Status in this library:* in force

(b) The trustee may avoid any transfer of an interest of the debtor in property— (1) to or for the benefit of a creditor; (2) for or on account of an antecedent debt; (3) made while the debtor was insolvent (presumed during the 90 days, §547(f)); (4) made **on or within 90 days before the date of the filing**; (5) that enables the creditor to receive more than in a chapter 7 liquidation. **(c)(2) Ordinary course:** the trustee may not avoid a transfer to the extent it was in payment of a debt incurred in the ordinary course and the transfer was made **(A) in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of the debtor and the transferee, or (B) according to ordinary business terms**. Payments made under **shortened terms, pressure, or unusual methods (wire on demand) compared with the parties' history** generally fall outside (c)(2)(A). **(c)(4) New value:** to the extent that, after such transfer, the creditor gave new value to or for the benefit of the debtor not secured and on account of which the debtor did not make an otherwise unavoidable transfer. (g) The creditor bears the burden on (c) defenses.

=== frbp_3002_3003.md ===
# Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002, 3003 — proofs of claim; bar date

*Citation:* Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3003(c)(2)-(3); 3002(c)  
*Status in this library:* in force

In a chapter 11 case, a creditor whose claim is not scheduled or is scheduled as disputed, contingent or unliquidated **must file a proof of claim** by the bar date fixed by the court; a creditor who fails to do so shall not be treated as a creditor for purposes of voting and distribution. Late claims are allowed only on a showing of excusable neglect (*Pioneer*). A §503(b)(9) request is typically made by motion or by the procedure the bar-date order specifies, and should be asserted separately from the general unsecured claim.

=== bc_502d_setoff.md ===
# 11 U.S.C. §502(d); setoff and recoupment

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §502(d); §553  
*Status in this library:* in force

§502(d): the court shall disallow any claim of an entity from which property is recoverable under §547 (preference) unless the entity has paid the amount for which it is liable. A creditor with preference exposure may find its claim disallowed until it returns the preference. Setoff of pre-petition mutual debts requires relief from stay.

=== critical_vendor_practice.md ===
# Critical vendor orders — practice note

*Citation:* *In re Kmart Corp.*, 359 F.3d 866 (7th Cir. 2004); Dkt. 44 in this case  
*Status in this library:* in force

A debtor may seek authority to pay certain pre-petition claims of vendors whose continued supply is essential and who cannot be replaced; the vendor must typically agree to customary trade terms for the case. Being designated a critical vendor is the legitimate route to early payment of pre-petition claims; it is at the debtor's discretion and the court's approval.
